newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's pension reforms seen boosting debt issues.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's pension reforms seen boosting debt issues.

text.p: Mexico's planned private pension scheme will spur the issuance of peso-denominated debt and help create a long-term capital market in Mexico, analysts and government officials said.
The Afores pension system plan is scheduled to start on January 1,1997.

Mexican financial groups, some in partnerships with foreign companies, are rushing to set up plans to cover millions of Mexican workers who until now have been forced to deal with the government pension plan.

An official with development bank Banco Nacional de Obras y Servicios Publicos told Reuters recently he believed the Afores scheme will allow them to extend terms on their peso paper beyond three years.
On Wednesday, Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz said in Washington the new social security system will draw between $3.0 billion and $4.0 billion in retirement savings next year.
In 20 to 25 year's time, the system is seen raising the equivalent of 40 percent of Mexico's gross domestic product, he said.
"This is important because this is the first time that Mexico will have a long-term capital market," Ortiz said.

During the first year of operation each Afore will be limited to one specialised investment fund, known as Siefores, with capitalization requirements. Moreover, a quantity of the peso-denomiated instruments willl have to be indexed to Mexico's consumer price index.
Pension regulatory commission Consar has said the investment restrictions were aimed at avoiding heavy loss.
At present, Mexico issues two inflation-linked instruments: Ajustabonos and Udibonos, but analysts expect more will be created.

"What they will surely offer at the start is public debt that has a return plus inflation. But the Afores will generate a dynamic in the capital markets that will create new instruments. Especially those that are more long term," said Humberto Allendes, market director for AFORE Santander, the fund being set up by Banco Santander.
Analysts said that much of the initial Afores purchases are expected to be government paper in order to help finance the health care and pension systems.
"At the beginning (the funds) will be invested in government paper that offers a real return," said ING Barings chief Mexico economist Sergio Martin.

"But there will be room for the Afores to buy paper that is not linked necessarily to inflation. You will be able to buy a certain amount of paper that is not inflation-linked, but gives a good return for the Afores," Martin said.
Corporate paper is also expected to be included in the investment packages.
About 17 Afores are expected to start seeking business on January 1 after the Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) loses its monopoly on the retirement funds of Mexican workers.
